items.title: Junior Mance Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995…
items.q: And then I’ve been working with another group called Lionel Hampton and the Golden Men of Jazz, which is an eight piece all star group.

ctx.x: And then I’ve been working with another group called Lionel Hampton and the Golden Men of Jazz, which is an eight piece all star group. It changes from time to time but usually it’s Al Grey on trombone, Clark Terry and Harry “Sweets” Edison on trumpets, James Moody usually on tenor saxophone, Grady Tate usually on drums, and Milt Hinton or Jimmy Woode on bass. You know and that’s you say “Golden Men” because we’re all over 60. I think that’s the criteria for being a member of this group. But they do mostly all…

know, he’s still got his big band going. The 29th of this month he’s going to do a gig with his big band. I said, oh, boy, I hope he doesn’t have another one, because we’re supposed to do some things in September. We’re going to a big jazz program at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles and they also are going to honor him again at the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C. And then other than that, well when school starts I’m a part time teacher. Whenever I’m there I teach. Because the faculty is made up of working…

items.title: Junior Mance Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 18, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: People like Woody Herman, Stan Kenton, some of Lionel Hampton’s book, even the Billy Eckstine Big Band.

ctx.x: Did you ever have occasion in those situations where someone would bring in a four page piece of music for the piano player, and you’re going “oh God, where’s the chord symbols?”

Oh, I feel the same way. I was never a fast sight reader. But you know as a kid I learned how to read music but it’s something that, you have to keep doing it. Once you stop, you’re going to not do it as well. And I stopped for years, because I went to the small band type way of playing. My reading was probably best right after high school and my first year of Roosevelt College. I was with this local big band, the one I was talking about that Gene Ammons played in. It was like the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis band of…

blues, maybe that’s something in the back of my mind as to why I don’t have that much music. I have some tunes you know. Occasionally I let them work on a bebop tune and let an ensemble do it, but other than that I just sort of got away from it. I was never that interested in getting back to it. I was never interested; and doing studio work, which is probably the most lucrative part of the business you know. Like look at the studio musicians now, even those into retirement, man they have pensions in five and six…

items.title: Lionel Hampton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

ctx.x: Buddy Tate is not playing. But maybe it will come to me after. We’ve got Sweets Edison playing one trumpet, and we’ve got Al Grey playing trombone and oh, this is all changed up.
Yeah. You’ve got Junior Mance on piano?
Yeah, Junior Mance on piano. And let me see. We’ve got the drummer, we’ve got, let’s see, oh, well.
